title: A House That Still Stands
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 31 of 40
content:
We returned to Spinner's End in March.

The house had survived winter.

Snape seemed offended by this.

“It leans,” he said from the pavement.

“It leaned before.”

“The eastern gutter has separated.”

“That is not structural collapse.”

“It is an invitation.”

“To rain?”

“To rot.”

“Very dramatic.”

“Very accurate.”

He unlocked the gate.

This time, I entered without needing to be asked twice.

That mattered.

So did the fact that he had invited me here for no professional reason at all.

The audit was finished.

The hearing was over.

Our relationship—still a word that made him look as if he had bitten tinfoil—had lasted two months without anyone dying, fleeing the country, or drafting a new statute.

Spinner's End was the first place we had come simply because it belonged to him.

Or had.

That was the question.

Inside, dust had reclaimed the furniture. The table no longer bore the word traitor. The sitting room still looked searched but not destroyed. Snape stood in the doorway with one hand in his coat pocket.

“I am considering selling it.”

I looked at the narrow room.

“Do you want to?”

“I dislike it.”

“That wasn't the question.”

His eyes narrowed.

I smiled.

“I learned from the best.”

“Debatable.”

We spent the morning opening windows.

Cold spring air moved through rooms that had been closed too long. I shook dust from curtains. Snape repaired the gutter from the upstairs window with a charm and then complained that Muggle architecture required magical intervention to become tolerable.

“You could just admit you're fixing your house.”

“I am preventing deterioration pending disposition.”

“Romantic.”

“Stop using that word incorrectly.”

I found a box beneath the stairs.

Not hidden.

Just forgotten.

Inside were old school things.

A Slytherin scarf.

Broken quills.

A chipped brass cauldron.

Several books with Severus Snape written inside in a cramped adolescent hand.

And a pair of boots far too small for the man standing behind me.

Snape went silent.

I looked at the boots.

Worn leather. Soles repaired twice. One lace replaced with cord.

“Yours?”

“Yes.”

“How old?”

“Eleven. Perhaps twelve.”

I touched one lightly.

“You kept them.”

“I forgot them.”

“Same result.”

His mouth tightened.

I did not say anything about poverty or neglect.

I did not need to narrate his childhood back to him.

I put the boots beside the box.

“Keep or discard?” I asked.

He looked surprised by the practical question.

“Discard.”

I put them in the discard pile.

He stared at them.

“Keep,” he said.

I moved them back.

Then he swore quietly.

I laughed.

“This is why people hate clearing houses.”

“It is irrational.”

“Probably.”

“They serve no purpose.”

“Neither does that terrible chair in your sitting room.”

“The chair is functional.”

“The chair is a threat.”

“It has survived forty years.”

“So has trauma. We don't praise everything for longevity.”

He gave me a look.

I grinned.

By lunch, we had three piles: keep, discard, undecided.

Undecided was largest.

Snape stood over it in disgust.

“This has accomplished nothing.”

“You opened the windows.”

“Heroic.”

“You fixed the gutter.”

“Necessary.”

“You found your school scarf.”

“Unfortunate.”

I picked it up.

Green and silver, faded almost gray.

“Put it down.”

I held it against his chest.

He went rigid.

“You looked adorable.”

“I will end you.”

“You were eleven.”

“I was never adorable.”

“That cannot possibly be true.”

He took the scarf from me and, after a pause, put it in the keep pile.

I smiled.

“Say nothing.”

“I am saying nothing.”

“Your face remains intolerable.”

We ate sandwiches in the kitchen.

The repaired table stood between us.

Snape had brought food from Hogwarts because he did not trust anything left in the cupboards.

I looked around.

“What would you do with the house if you kept it?”

“Nothing.”

“That seems wasteful.”

“It is a house, not an assignment.”

“Could be a laboratory.”

His eyes lifted.

The idea had occurred to him.

Interesting.

“A small one,” I continued. “Independent research. No students. No Board. No Ministry except when they inevitably annoy you.”

“Ventilation is poor.”

“So fix it.”

“Plumbing is worse.”

“Magic.”

“The cellar floods.”

“Drainage charm.”

“You have an irritating answer for everything.”

“You taught me.”

He looked away, but not before I saw interest.

“Why here?” he asked.

That was the real question.

Why build anything new in a place that held so much old pain?

I considered.

“You don't have to.”

His shoulders eased.

“But keeping it wouldn't mean the childhood wins,” I continued. “Selling it wouldn't mean you escaped. It's just property unless you decide otherwise.”

Snape stared at the tabletop.

“Just a house,” he said.

“Potentially a judgmental one.”

His mouth twitched.

We spent the afternoon in the back room measuring shelves.

Not because he had decided.

He repeatedly informed me he had not decided.

Then he drew three laboratory layouts on scrap parchment.

The first used the existing cellar.

The second expanded the kitchen wall.

The third converted the sitting room into a library and built a separate workroom in the yard.

“You haven't decided,” I said.

“Correct.”

“Very undecided drawings.”

“They are feasibility studies.”

“Of course.”

He handed me the third.

“What?”

“Your opinion.”

I looked at him.

“Mine?”

“You have one. Constantly.”

“Do you want it?”

He hesitated.

“Yes.”

I studied the plan.

“The separate workroom.”

“Why?”

“More light. Better ventilation. You could keep the house as a house instead of turning every room into proof of productivity.”

His eyes narrowed.

“That last statement was unnecessary.”

“Still true.”

He took the plan back.

The late sun angled through the window.

For once, Spinner's End did not look gray.

Dust moved gold in the light.

Snape stood beside the old desk where he had once watched for Lily.

I wondered whether he was seeing the past.

Then he looked at me.

“Would you come here?” he asked.

The question sounded casual only if one knew nothing about him.

“To the laboratory?”

“To the house.”

My heart turned over.

“Yes.”

“For work?”

“Sometimes.”

His mouth tightened.

“And otherwise?”

I stepped closer.

“Yes.”

The answer was enough.

Snape's hand touched my waist.

“Still judgmental?” he asked.

“The house?”

“Yes.”

“Less so.”

“Why?”

“Better company.”

He kissed me in the room where he had once waited at the window for someone else.

That did not erase the boy.

It did not replace Lily.

It did not transform the house into a symbol of healing because life was rarely that courteous.

It was simply a new memory.

The house still stood.

So did he.

For the moment, that was enough.

prose_fingerprint: emotionally direct without flattening emotion into exposition
ground abstract feelings in concrete physical details, objects, weather, rooms, gestures, and sensory anchors
alternate compact emotional beats with fuller reflective paragraphs
let dialogue carry relationship pressure while narration carries interior consequence
use humor and ordinary practical actions to make vulnerable scenes feel lived-in rather than staged
favor character-specific reactions and small remembered details over generic declarations
allow grief, identity, survival, belonging, home, change, vulnerability, care, and autonomy to recur as thematic pressure
end scenes or chapters on an emotional consequence, changed understanding, concrete image, callback, or forward pull
preserve first-person immediacy and avoid omniscient knowledge outside Jasper's perception
use semicolons selectively for linked thoughts rather than mechanically
dialogue_fingerprint: continuous dialogue should sound conversational rather than like alternating speeches
interrupt dialogue with gestures, environment, hesitation, humor, and internal reaction
let characters dodge, misunderstand, tease, repair, and return to earlier wording
do not make every character equally eloquent, equally dominant, or equally emotionally transparent
relationship_fingerprint: slow burn must accumulate evidence: remembered preferences, repaired conflict, shared routines, private jokes, and practical care
attraction should not erase plot, outside obligations, individual goals, or conflict
vulnerability is strongest when it changes later behavior
after an intense/private interlude, resume with reconnection, humor, care, consequences, memory updates, and the next plot beat rather than treating intimacy as a reset
